svg.aria-label: Animated diagram. One decision, a record naming 'Boom BK' with two candidates and 'none', shown to five kinds of decision model: a label classifier that scores each option label; option-marker encoders that score a marker token placed before each option; decoders that list lettered options and read the next-token scores of the letters; a pointer head that compares each option's closing token with a final decide token; and models that write one prompt per option and ask whether it is correct.

g.text: Every model gets the same decision: a record, its candidates, and the option ‘none’.
A label classifier reads the options as labels and scores each one against the record.
Option-marker encoders put a marker before each option and score the markers in one pass.
Lettered prompts list the options as A, B, C and read how strongly the model would answer each letter.
A pointer head compares a final ‘decide’ token with the end of each option.
Or ask once per option: ‘is this the right answer?’, and compare the yes-scores.
One encoder pass over labels + text; a small network scores each label.
Options and their descriptions are part of the label list.
One encoder pass; the score is read at each option's marker.
von and bekko stop the options from seeing each other.
Read once, at the end: how much the model wants to say A, B or C.
JEV and GEV read a trained 24-slot head there instead of the letters.
Each option's closing token is compared with the final decide token.
Options are wrapped in reserved tokens the text can't contain.
WHAT THE MODEL READS · THREE TIMES
Simple and accurate, but the record is read once per candidate.
Ten candidates means ten passes: the slowest design to train.
Bars are illustrative, not model output.
